articles.title: When a 19th-Century Scottish Landowner Blocked a Public Footpath, Locals Rebelled. Now, Archaeologists Have Unearthed Parts of His Controversial Wall

paras.en: Archaeologists in Scotland have unearthed the remains of a controversial structure near Glasgow that was the nexus of a violent 1823 clash over land rights and private property.

In the early 19th century, a wealthy Scottish distiller named Thomas Harvie bought an estate in the countryside just east of Glasgow. Taking issue with a public pathway along the River Clyde that cut through his property, Harvie built two 12-foot-tall, heavily fortified walls on either side of his estate, blocking the public from using the path. The walls became known as Harvie’s Dyke, a Scottish term for a stone wall.

“The people of Glasgow [were] quite up in arms against this,” Edward Stewart, an archaeologist with Archaeology Scotland, tells the Scotsman in a video. In 1823, a mob of discontented locals from the East End of Glasgow marched to Harvie’s Dyke and destroyed the walls with gunpowder and explosives that coalminers brought from the mines.

A militia dispersed the mob and arrested participants. Harvie rebuilt his walls, topping them with iron spikes, broken glass and small cannons. But the Glaswegians fought back again, this time through a lawsuit that reached as far as the House of Lords. In 1828, the Lords ruled in favor of the people of Glasgow, and Harvie was forced to install gates in the dike to establish the public right of way through his property.

This year, archaeologists and volunteers took part in “Digging the Dyke”—a collaborative excavation organized by the Glasgow Building Preservation Trust, Glasgow City Council, Glasgow Life and Archaeology Scotland—at a location along the River Clyde where historical records suggest Harvie’s eastern wall once stood.

The excavation unearthed what researchers believe are foundations of the demolished wall, as well as a rare 1791 token engraved with the phrase “Let Glasgow Flourish,” per a statement. Opponents of the dike in the 1820s adopted that slogan as a rallying cry, suggesting that the coin may have been purposefully dropped near the site. Researchers also discovered pieces of mortar, slate and plasterwork that may have composed one of the dike’s defensive structures.

As Glaswegians rallied against Harvie’s Dyke, Harvie became a “pariah figure,” per the statement. The public boycotted his whiskey, and Harvie frittered away his fortune on legal bills. “Harvie never really recovers from this,” Stewart tells the Scotsman. “All because of his hubris and his unwillingness to allow people to take access through his land.”
Meanwhile, the people of Glasgow rejoiced. Their 1828 victory against Harvie inspired poems, songs and commemorative medals.

“The Harvie’s Dyke protesters had developed a green consciousness long before the Green Party was established,” Christopher Whatley, an emeritus historian at the University of Dundee and author of Harvie's Dyke: The People, Their Liberty and the Clyde, tells the Herald’s Jody Harrison.
Later, the campaign against Harvie’s Dyke was evoked throughout the 19th century to prevent landowners from blocking long-used walkways, Whatley said in a 2025 lecture.

“Let the people remember the famous battles of Harvie’s Dyke and take courage,” wrote the Glasgow Weekly Herald in 1884. “That the banks of the Clyde should be free … is in cause a matter of life and death to our humbler citizens, who are in growing danger of suffocation from want of pure air in the city and free spaces in the country.”

articles.title: Scientists Don't Know How Mars Acquired Its Two Moons. Japan Just Launched a Historic Space Mission That Will Fetch Samples to Find Out

paras.en: The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) is sending a spacecraft toward Mars to help solve an enduring mystery of the solar system: Where did the Red Planet’s two lunar companions, Phobos and Deimos, come from?

JAXA’s Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe launched from the agency’s Tanegashima Space Center in southern Japan on October 20 at 4:41 a.m. local time (October 19 at 3:41 p.m. Eastern time). If all goes according to plan, the Japan-led mission will bring samples from Phobos, the larger of the lunar duo, back to Earth in five years. These precious bits of dirt could finally reveal how the moon and its smaller sibling came to be, while also shedding light on Mars’ history.

“Despite their potential importance, Martian moons have never been fully investigated,” JAXA planetary scientist and MMX project manager Yasuhiro Kawakatsu tells the Associated Press’ Mari Yamaguchi. “They are known as the most important unclimbed mountains in the solar system.”

There are two main hypotheses about Phobos and Deimos’ creation. One posits they may have formed the same way Earth’s own moon formed: Something slammed into Mars and shot tons of material into space, which eventually coalesced into the two moons. (Why this would have birthed dual mini moons, rather than a single large one like Earth’s, remains an open question.) The other possible explanation suggests that the two bodies were asteroids sucked into Mars’ orbit millions of years ago, according to a statement from NASA, which is contributing to MMX. Other collaborators include the European Space Agency, France’s National Center for Space Studies, the German Aerospace Center and the Australian Space Agency.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Both scenarios carry significance for understanding their host planet. If Phobos formed from Martian debris, it could be made of material from Mars’ earlier days, when the Red Planet may have been better predisposed to host life than it is now, according to a JAXA statement. On the other hand, if Phobos hails from the far reaches of the solar system, it may have brought along water-bearing minerals and organics that could’ve helped birth life on Earth.

Scientists are hoping that the MMX mission, which is slated to reach Mars’ system in August of next year, will help solve the matter. The spacecraft will first investigate Phobos from orbit before landing on the moon’s surface twice in separate locations to collect the highly anticipated samples. The MMX probe will also investigate Mars from a distance and perform flyby observations of Deimos.

“We’re going to choose a first landing site and then do some landing operations, and after that we’re going to lift off and get back to orbit,” Tomohiro Usui, a JAXA planetary scientist and member of the MMX team, tells CNN’s Ashley Strickland. “It takes another several months for the search of the next landing site. Landing operations are very risky.”

The mission will collect samples on Phobos via two instruments. One will collect ground surface samples by acting like a vacuum cleaner. It’ll emit bursts of high-pressure nitrogen gas to loosen the dirt and suck up the disturbed regolith. The other sampler will pull cores from a few inches deeper in the ground. Only 0.35 ounces of material will be transported back to Earth, but that’s plenty for scientists to work with, Chrysa Avdellidou, a planetary scientist at the University of Leicester in England who is working on the mission, tells BBC News’ Rebecca Morelle, Alison Francis and Kevin Church.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “We can do several studies even on individual grains. … You don’t need to have kilos back from a surface in order to do science. So, it’s worth every gram,” she tells the outlet.

If MMX is successful, it would become the first mission to return a sample from a Martian moon, and it could be the first to complete a round trip from the Martian system. And because scientists suspect Phobos has gotten sprayed with debris from asteroid impacts on Mars, the returned samples could include bits of the Red Planet. Phobos was chosen as the landing destination mainly because it’s the moon closest to the host planet, and therefore more likely to have Martian dust, reports the AP.

Only 1 percent of the material collected might be from Mars, Kiyoshi Kuramoto, a planetary scientist at Hokkaido University in Japan and MMX team member, tells Science’s Robin George Andrews. Still, that tiny fraction of otherworldly dirt might carry evidence of extraterrestrial life. “I do think there’s a possibility that chemical traces of biological activity might be contained within that sand sample,” Kuramoto says.

articles.title: The Burning of This French City Hall Was a 'Catastrophe for Heritage,' Tragically Reminiscent of the Notre-Dame Fire

paras.en: Since it first opened its doors on Bastille Day in 1883, the city hall of Limoges, France, has been celebrated as an architectural wonder. Well known for its tall spire and ornate metal belfry, the 143-year-old building gained historic monument status in 1975 as a prime example of late 19th-century French architecture and civic pride.

On the building’s parapet, the city’s coat of arms was framed by mosaic portraits of four famous former residents, who lived in Limoges between the 16th and 19th centuries: Leonard Limosin, an enamel painter; Henri François d’Aguesseau, a jurist who served as a chancellor of France; Pierre Victurnien Vergniaud, an orator and figure of the French Revolution; and Jean-Baptiste, Count Jourdan, a military commander and one of Napoleon’s marshals.

But this weekend, much of the city hall was destroyed in a blaze that French authorities immediately characterized as arson. Amid antigovernment protests that have gripped France in recent days, masked individuals forced their way into the building on Saturday evening and set fires that spread to cause extensive damage, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP).

“Today, the entire facade and the historic front section have been almost 100 percent destroyed,” Maurice Barate, a top regional official, said on national television, per the New York Times’ Giulia Imbert. The spire and roof also collapsed. Barate called the arson a “catastrophe for heritage” and a “deliberate act by hooligans,” according to AFP.

The physical extent and emotional toll of the town hall’s damage was immediately compared to that of Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris, which burned extensively in 2019, likely as the result of an accident, not deliberate arson. Over 12 hours, the inferno destroyed most of the 12th-century cathedral’s roof, spire and exterior decorations, though many religious relics and artworks inside were salvaged.

The Notre-Dame tragedy struck an emotional chord not only in France but around the world. Donors raised close to $1 billion to support the cathedral’s reconstruction. In 2023, a new spire was raised, and in late 2024, it officially reopened to the public.
“It broke my heart. I saw Notre-Dame all over again, except this time it was our town,” Francoise Faurie, a Limoges resident who witnessed the fire, tells Reuters’ Clotaire Achi.

Leaders are calling for monetary support from the French government. “I want us to have the same capacity to rebuild as was given to Notre-Dame de Paris,” Guillaume Guérin, the mayor of Limoges, told local media, per the Telegraph’s Vivian Song. “I want to see a rain of millions on the city.”

In the blaze’s aftermath, fire crews and other emergency personnel continue to monitor the building for possible signs of collapse and other infrastructural weaknesses. Standing further back, residents have come to pay their respects to the building, which was a popular location for events such as baptisms and wedding ceremonies.

“All we have left are pictures,” Gilles Peignelin, who married his wife in the building, told the New York Times as he stood beside her and looked at the ruins. “I’m outraged—it’s shameful, deplorable.”

articles.title: French leaders impose curfews after weekend of protests, violence

paras.en: Oct. 19 (UPI) -- Authorities in parts of France have imposed curfews Monday as the country recovered from widespread protests over the weekend that turned violent in places.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu asked some cities to establish "partial curfews" in response to the events, in which at least two people killed and more than 2,000 were arrested.

The curfews include one from 11 p.m. Monday to 6 a.m. Tuesday local time in Paris' Place de la République and another from 10 p.m. Monday to 6 a.m. in the streets around Les Halle, CNN reported. There are other curfews in Lyon, Marseille, Nice and other cities and communities.

The protests started in September with high students demonstrating for better school and education conditions. The protests spread to university students, union leaders and others concerned about the cost of living, remaining mostly peaceful.

Over the weekend, however, things turned more violent in places. Some rioters took to vandalism, setting buildings on fire, breaking windows and looting from shops. These incidents took place in major cities across the country, including Paris, Limoges, Bourdeaux, Grenoble, Nice, Marseille, Lyon, Rennes and Strasbourg.
French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday asked for calm, saying that the "legitimate demands" of students had been hijacked by looters and those causing destruction.
"I've asked the government to provide all the lessons learned and to be able to anticipate it to make sure that this does not happen again," he said. "We need unity, we need calm and respect."
Earlier Monday, Macron rejected French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez's offer to resign after the protests.

A statement from the Élysée Palace, the office of the presidency, said Macron refused Nuñez's offer "given the need for continuous command of the security forces in the current situation." Macron, instead, asked Nuñez to employ "new methods of action on the ground as quickly as possible ... against violent rioters," EuroNews reported.
Macron said he planned to hold meetings this week to address protestors' concerns and demands.

Lecornu said the government will set aside money to help affected areas recover from the damage and that there will be a partial unemployment fund for those unable to work due to the riots and looting.
The head of France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry said more than 2,000 shops and other businesses have been affected and that damages were at hundreds of millions of euros.
In the United States, meanwhile, President Donald Trump and J.D. Vance blamed the riots on immigration.
"The migrants have taken over France," Trump wrote in a social media post Monday morning. "They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!"
Over the weekend, meanwhile, Vance said he hoped that Americans were paying attention to the violence in France and claimed that "this is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country."

articles.title: DHS: Ukrainians, Sudanese remain shielded from deportation for now

paras.en: Oct. 19 (UPI) -- The Department of Homeland Security said Monday that more than 100,000 Ukrainians and Sudanese in the United States would remain shielded from deportation for the time being under a humanitarian immigration program that the Trump administration has sought to curtail.

Both Ukraine and Sudan have been designated for Temporary Protected Status, a program that prevents eligible nationals already in the United States from being deported to their home countries that are experiencing life-threatening conditions due to war or natural disasters.

The previous Biden administration extended TPS protections for El Salvador, Sudan, Ukraine and Venezuela for 18 months during its final days before leaving office to the Trump administration, which has announced terminations of TPS designations for 13 countries, including Venezuela, though litigation has blocked some terminations from taking effect.
TPS for Sudan and Ukraine was to expire Monday.
DHS did not state it was extending TPS for either country, but that "an announcement" concerning their statuses "will be made at the appropriate time."
Until the announcement is made, Ukrainians and Sudanese present in the United States under TPS will "retain protection including work authorization."
There are about 103,700 Ukrainians and 1,900 Sudanese TPS beneficiaries, according to government estimates.

Ending TPS, arguing the protection was only supposed to be temporary, has been among tactics of the Trump administration's execution of its hardline immigration crackdown, raising the prospects of deportation for immigrants, some of whom have lived in the United States for decades under the TPS program.
"We're grateful for an extensions, however temporary, for TPS holders from Ukraine and Sudan," Myal Greene, president and CEO of World Relief, said in a statement Monday.

The Christian humanitarian organization has been among those calling on Congress to pass legislation creating long-term legal protections for those who cannot return to the war-ravaged countries such as Ukraine and Sudan, rather than creating an atmosphere of uncertainty for those who wait to learn whether their TPS status will be renewed.

"TPS is intended to be temporary, but unfortunately, conflict and instability don't respect our preferred timelines," Matthew Soerens, vice president of advocacy and policy at World Relief, said in the statement.
"We're grateful that Ukrainian and Sudanese TPS holders can go a bit longer without fear of having to return to war zones, but that relief is fleeting."

Daniel Delgado, former deputy assistant secretary for immigration policy at DHS under the Biden administration and current senior policy fellow at the Washington, D.C.-based Searchlight Institute, criticized the Trump administration on Monday for leaving the Sudanese and Ukrainian TPS-protected individuals in limbo by not making a decision on their status.

"Instead of clear guidance to help inform the life-altering decisions that thousands of Ukrainians and Sudanese will be forced to make, DHS and this administration would rather they live with an increasing sense of uncertainty and anxiety," Delgado said in a statement on social media.
"There's a process in place to determine whether a country warrants TPS. It is a choice to not follow it."
The Biden administration initially designated Ukraine for TPS following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Sudan has had TPS status since 1997, though the first Trump administration unsuccessfully sought to terminate its designation. The Biden administration then issued a new designation for Sudan in March 2022 amid a political and humanitarian crisis in the African nation following an October 2021 military coup that preceded the outbreak of the country's ongoing civil war in April 2023.

articles.title: More lawmakers say they were targets of suspicious mail

paras.en: Oct. 19 (UPI) -- More than a dozen U.S. lawmakers announced Monday that suspicious envelopes had been sent to their offices, joining dozens of colleagues already targeted by similar mailings, many containing white powder, just weeks before November's midterm elections.
The letters, first reported Tuesday, have been sent to lawmakers from both political parities across the nation.

Lawmakers who announced Monday that suspicious letters had been sent to their offices included Reps. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va.; Joe Neguse, D-Colo.; Jason Crow, D-Colo.; Brittany Pettersen, D-Colo.; Diana DeGette, D-Colo.; Chellie Pingree, D-Maine; Debbie Wasserman Schultz, D-Fla.; Becca Balint, D-Vt.; Greg Stanton, D-Ariz.; Adam Smith, D-Wash.; Adam Smith, D-Wash.; Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz.; and Adelita Grijalva, D-Ariz.
Senators who announced Monday that letters had been sent to their offices included John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., and Ron Johnson, R-Wis.
Some of the suspicious envelopes did arrive at the lawmakers' offices while others were intercepted by postal investigators.

"I can confirm that my office in Leesburg received an envelope containing a suspicious substance," Subramanyam wrote on social media Monday afternoon. "The office was promptly evacuated. Thank you to the Leesburg Police, Loudoun County Fire and Rescue and their Hazmat team and the Capitol Police for their swift response.
"These acts of political intimidation have no place in our country," he wrote.

Johnson said the suspicious envelope was delivered to his Milwaukee office at 2:38 p.m. CT Monday. He said the return address matched the description of letters sent to the offices of other lawmakers, though he did not make public what the address was.
"My staff immediately isolated the envelope, cleared all staff members and called 911 and the Sergeant at Arms," he said on social media.
"The first responders confiscated the letter, and thankfully, everyone is safe. Our office operations have now resumed as normal."
Both Pingree and Wasserman Schultz published pictures online of the suspicious letters their offices received, showing that the addresses were handwritten.
"Such cowardly acts of coercion will not work and have absolutely no place in our politics," Wasserman Schultz said in a statement.
"And to be clear, they will not deter me from fully representing my Broward County constituents."

While the return address of the letter Wasserman Schultz posted online was redacted, the letter posted by Pingree was not and bears a New York City address formerly used by the Democratic Socialists of America.
DSA spokesperson Priscilla Yeverino has previously said in a statement that the group is not involved in the letters in any way.
"We are glad to learn no one was harmed," she said.

Other lawmakers who have reported such incidents include Reps. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., and Eugene Vindman, D-Va., and Sens. Adam Schiff, D-Calif.; Pete Ricketts, R-Neb.; Ted Cruz, R-Texas; and Mike Rounds, R-S.D., among others of both major parties.
Schiff said Sunday that at least one envelope containing a suspicious substance was sent to his offices in California and was intercepted by U.S. Capitol Police and the Senate Sergeant at Arms.

"This attempt to intimidate elected officials and our staff will not succeed," Schiff said. "We instead condemn these threats as antithetical to the values of our nation, recommit to our work and thank the law enforcement and postal officials who are helping keep our teams safe."

The incidents apparently started Tuesday, when Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry and the Oklahoma State Election Board reported receiving envelopes with a similar white powder. The Senate Sergeant at Arms, Capitol Police, FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating.

articles.title: REPUBLIC Rules the Billboard 200 Top 10 With 8 Albums, Led by Taylor Swift
articles.author: Keith Caulfield

paras.en: REPUBLIC rules the top 10 of the Billboard 200 albums chart (dated Oct. 24) as, for a third time, the label is home to eight of the top 10 titles. Since Luminate’s electronically monitored music data began powering the list on May 25, 1991, REPUBLIC is the only label to have held at least eight of the top 10 titles. The company did it for the first time on the Jan. 13, 2024-dated list, and then again one week later.

In the top 10 of the latest Billboard 200, REPUBLIC — and its group of labels — has the following albums: Taylor Swift’s The Life of a Showgirl (on Republic Records) at No. 1, Morgan Wallen’s I’m the Problem (released via Big Loud/Mercury) at No. 3, Noah Kahan’s The Great Divide (Mercury) at No. 5, Drake’s HABIBTI (OVO Sound/Republic Records) at No. 6, Olivia Dean’s The Art of Loving (Polydor/Island) at No. 7, Kahan’s Stick Season (Mercury) at No. 8, Greta Van Fleet’s Palace for the People (Lava/Republic Records) at No. 9 and Drake’s ICEMAN (OVO Sound/Republic Records) at No. 10.

articles.title: A Very ‘Glee’ Reunion! Darren Criss Makes Debut at London’s Royal Albert Hall With Surprise Chris Colfer Duet: ‘It’s Been Awhile’
articles.author: Katie Atkinson

paras.en: Anyone who was introduced to Darren Criss through his role on Glee was in for a special treat Sunday night (Oct. 18) at London’s Royal Albert Hall, where the Emmy- and Tony-winning actor reunited with co-star Chris Colfer to perform together for the first time in more than a decade.

Criss joined Glee during season 2 in 2010 to play Blaine Anderson, the lead singer of the Dalton Academy Warblers and love interest (and eventual first boyfriend) for Colfer’s Kurt Hummel. On Sunday, when Criss made his debut at the iconic venue with two back-to-back performances, Colfer was among an impressive lineup of surprise guests who hit the stage.

But before Colfer arrived, Criss teased the crowd by attempting to sing one of Kurt and Blaine’s most memorable duets all by himself: “Baby, It’s Cold Outside,” from the season 2 episode “A Very Glee Christmas,” which peaked at No. 57 on the Billboard Hot 100 back in 2010. “I’m gonna do my best to sing both parts,” he told the audience, launching into the impossible solo duet. A few lines in, though, the crowd started cheering when they saw Colfer emerge.

“Hey, Darren!” Colfer casually said, to which Criss responded: “It’s been awhile!” In fact, the pair hadn’t performed together in more than a decade, given Glee wrapped its seven-season run back in 2015.
“Do you know the words to this?” Criss prompted Colfer, who assured him: “I do.”

In addition to the Colfer surprise, other surprise guests included Alan Cumming for ABBA’s “Does Your Mother Know”; Stranger Things star Gaten Matarazzo for “Lost Boys Life,” an original song Criss wrote and recorded with his late brother, Chuck Criss, for their band Computer Games; Sarah Hyland for “Suddenly Seymour” from Little Shop of Horrors; as well as her Modern Family co-star Jesse Tyler Ferguson for Adele’s “Someone Like You.”

Even before Criss was on Glee, he made a name for himself as a University of Michigan student by co-creating A Very Potter Musical, a Harry Potter-themed musical that went viral online. On Sunday night, he performed “Goin’ Back to Hogwarts” from the show joined by an ensemble of acclaimed stage performers, including Glee’s Alex Newell (Shucked, Once on This Island), Jak Malone (Operation Mincemeat), Natasha Hodgson (Operation Mincemeat) and Andrew Barth Feldman (Dear Evan Hansen, Little Shop of Horrors).

articles.title: Swae Lee Announces 2027 Australian Same Difference Tour
articles.author: Jessica Lynch

paras.en: Swae Lee is heading back to Australia. The rapper and singer has announced a five-date national tour for January 2027 in support of his debut solo album, Same Difference.

The Australian run opens Jan. 6 at Melbourne’s Forum before heading to Sydney’s Enmore Theatre on Jan. 8 and Brisbane’s Fortitude Music Hall on Jan. 10. Shows at Adelaide’s Hindley Street Music Hall and Perth’s Metro City follow on Jan. 12 and Jan. 13, respectively.

Presented by Live Nation, the dates follow a run of European shows throughout late 2026 and arrive after the release of Same Difference, Swae Lee’s first full-length solo studio album, feauturing Post Malone, Jhené Aiko and French Montana among its collaborators.

The album marks a significant solo milestone for an artist whose voice has been attached to some of the biggest crossover records of the past decade. Swae Lee first rose to prominence alongside his brother Slim Jxmmi in Rae Sremmurd, with the duo scoring their first Billboard Hot 100 No. 1 in 2016 when “Black Beatles,” featuring Gucci Mane, spent seven weeks atop the chart.
His success continued outside the duo. French Montana’s “Unforgettable,” featuring Swae Lee, reached No. 3 on the Hot 100 in 2017, becoming Swae Lee’s first top 10 as a solo artist.

A year later, he teamed with Post Malone for “Sunflower” from Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse. The song reached No. 1 on the Hot 100 in January 2019, giving Swae Lee his first chart-topper as a solo artist. It ultimately spent 33 weeks in the top 10, becoming one of the most enduring hits of its era.

Swae Lee also has a songwriting credit on Travis Scott’s “Sicko Mode,” which topped the Hot 100 in December 2018. Those collaborations helped establish him as one of hip-hop’s most recognizable melodic voices even before the arrival of his first solo LP.
The Live Nation presale begins Thursday, Oct. 22, at 9 a.m. AEDT, with general tickets going on sale Friday, Oct. 23, at 10 a.m. AEDT.

articles.title: ‘Star Wars’-Themed Super Bowl Altcast Joins Disney’s Big Game Lineup
articles.author: Rick Porter

paras.en: The 2027 Super Bowl will take place at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California — and also a galaxy far, far away.

Lucasfilm, ESPN, Disney and the NFL will present an animated, real(ish)-time alternate telecast of Super Bowl LXI set in the Star Wars universe. The altcast will stream in Disney+ and the ESPN app and air on Disney Channel and Disney XD alongside the main broadcast (on ABC, ESPN and Disney+) and several other alternate presentations.

Disney has done a few animated altcasts, which it calls “Funday Football,” in the past few years. Prior telecasts have featured characters from Toy Story, The Simpsons and Monsters Inc. Those all took place alongside regular-season NFL games, however — not the biggest single broadcast in any given year.

The Star Wars version the game will feature Anthony Daniels voicing C-3PO. Other characters from the franchise will also appear. The game’s real-life players will be translated into animated avatars, with Star Wars characters subbing in for key plays. Sony’s Beyond Sports provides the data visualization tech that powers the animated presentation.

The Star Wars altcast will run alongside additional alternate Super Bowl presentations on ESPN2, ESPNU and NFL Network. Disney will also bring Star Wars to the NFL some during the regular season: Starting Tuesday, SC+ — the streaming version of SportsCenter that runs on Disney+ — will feature Monday Night Football highlights “with a Star Wars visual theme,” according to a press release. Beginning with the Oct. 26 MNF game, SC+ will also have an animated Darth Vader interview a player in that week’s contest.

articles.title: Mariah Carey $20 Million Defamation Lawsuit Over Memoir Dismissed
articles.author: Jackie Strause

paras.en: Mariah Carey on Monday won a long-running $20 million lawsuit alleging she defamed her brother in her bestselling memoir The Meaning of Mariah Carey when a New York state court dismissed the suit.

Morgan Carey, brother to the iconic singer, first filed his lawsuit on May 28, 2021, claiming Mariah damaged his reputation in the 2020 memoir by portraying him as violent and accusing him of trafficking cocaine. In the ruling issued Monday, reported by Billboard and Rolling Stone, Justice Leslie A. Stroth of the New York State Supreme Court found that Morgan Carey failed to establish that his sister acted with actual malice.

“Plaintiff has not sufficiently pleaded actual malice on the part of [Mariah],” Justice Stroth wrote, according to the reported ruling. “Plaintiff fails to provide any proof that [Mariah] made such statements with knowledge of their falsity or with reckless disregard of their falsity or with reckless disregard for the truth. While plaintiff alleges that [Mariah] demonstrates ill will towards her brother, such statement is insufficient, and plaintiff has not satisfied the pleading requirement for actual malice.”

articles.title: Ann Hornaday, Longtime Washington Post Film Critic, Dies at 66
articles.author: Abid Rahman

paras.en: Ann Hornaday, the longtime film critic at The Washington Post and author, died Sunday. She was 66.
Hornaday died at her home in North Baltimore after a battle with glioblastoma, a form of brain cancer, her husband Dennis Greenia told the Baltimore Banner.
A much-loved and respected film critic, Hornaday was named a Pulitzer Prize finalist for criticism in 2008.

Born March 9, 1960, in Iowa City, Iowa, Hornaday grew up in Des Moines. She graduated from Smith College in 1982 with a degree in government and later moved to New York. She freelanced for Premiere, Us and worked at the feminist publication Ms. Magazine, and became co-founder Gloria Steinem’s administrative assistant.

After taking a journalism fellowship in Athens, Georgia, where she met her husband, Hornaday would go on to work at various newspapers, including the Austin American-Statesman and The Baltimore Sun, before joining The Washington Post in 2002, replacing previous critic Rita Kempley.

At the Post she became a national figure in film criticism writing hundreds of reviews, and was known for her accessible reviews that were free of pretension. During her run as a prominent critic, she also appeared on WYPR’s Midday at the Movies program. She left the Post in 2025 after taking a buyout.

In 2017, she wrote the book Talking Pictures: How to Watch Movies, a practical guide for movie lovers on how to appreciate cinema and improve film literacy. Hornaday had also completed a book about the production of Alan J. Pakula’s classic 1976 political thriller All the President’s Men. That book is set to be published posthumously in 2028.
Hornaday is survived by her husband Dennis, daughters Victoria and Leila, and brother William.

articles.title: BlackRock, GIC among investors chasing Indian telecom major Jio's IPO as anchor bids top $26 billion

paras.en: The country's largest telecommunications and digital services company, backed by Meta and Google, plans to raise up to 302 billion rupees ($3.2 billion) through India's largest ever IPO in rupee terms.

According to the source, who is not allowed to speak on the matter due to legal restrictions, the company's anchor book received total bids worth 2.5 trillion rupees ($26.3 billion) for the 81.1 billion rupee anchor book portion.
Jio Platforms, in a release on Monday, said it had finalized the allocation of 72.47 million equity shares to anchor investors at 1,119 rupees a share, at the upper range of the price band.
The anchor book is a portion of the total fundraise set aside for large institutional investors before the IPO opens for public bidding.

Some other major institutional investors who have been allocated shares include India's state-owned insurance firm Life Insurance Corporation, Fidelity Investments, JPMorgan Asset Management and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority.

The Jio Platforms IPO will be open to the public from Wednesday through Friday. Jio Platforms, owned by Reliance Industries, has been positioning itself as a tech company and not just a traditional utility provider. The IPO price values the company at around $108 billion — lower than the valuations of over $130 billion floated a year ago.

articles.title: Bank Indonesia faces mounting pressure to hike after MSCI threat fuels market rout

paras.en: Bank Indonesia faces mounting pressure to raise interest rates on Wednesday as economists revise their forecasts after global index provider MSCI warned it may downgrade the country's stock market from emerging-market status, setting off a selloff in stocks and the rupiah.

Citibank now expects a pre-emptive 50 basis-point increase to 6.25%, abandoning its earlier call for no change. Capital Economics and Permata Bank expect a 25 basis-point hike to 6%. The central bank has held its benchmark seven-day reverse repurchase rate at 5.75% since June.

MSCI said Friday it is considering moving Indonesia to "standalone" from the emerging-market status it has held since 1989, causing the Jakarta Composite Index to suffer the worst two-day sell-off recorded, before recovering about 3% Tuesday after authorities announced steps to improve market transparency and price discovery, including expelling tightly held companies from the flagship index.
Meanwhile, rupiah weakened to 18,030 per dollar on Tuesday, near its June record low, falling about 8% this year.

"Not delivering a rate hike [on Wednesday] would run the risk of disappointing investors and fueling further downward pressure on the currency," said Jason Tuvey, deputy chief emerging markets economist at Capital Economics. "A decision to hold rates on Wednesday could also revive concerns among investors that Bank Indonesia is kowtowing to political pressure."

Citi's Helmi Arman said a hike would aim to stop equity outflows spilling into bonds and prompting capital flight by domestic investors. He expects it to be a "one-off" followed by other support such as government foreign-currency borrowing or another round of bilateral currency swaps with foreign central banks.

The central bank has already raised rates by a combined 100 basis points since May. Headline inflation quickened to a three-month high of 3.28% in September, within the 1.5%-3.5% target range, while core inflation eased to 2.84%. The governor, Destry Damayanti, has said foreign-exchange reserves of $146.3 billion at the end of September would be adequate to stabilize the rupiah.

"Market confidence can deteriorate much faster than economic fundamentals," said Josua Pardede, chief economist at PT Bank Permata, estimating that foreign investors have net sold about $5 billion of Indonesian stocks this year. The risk is that foreign equity withdrawals could further weaken the rupiah and trigger selling in government bonds, he added.

An MSCI downgrade could force $3 billion to $5 billion of passive outflows, with another $15 billion of actively managed foreign money exposed to reassessment, he estimates. Pardede expects the market adjustment may come in stages, from precautionary selling through the first half of 2027 and mechanical selling if MSCI confirms the move by June.

"BI can provide liquidity and reduce excessive volatility, but only credible market-governance reforms can address MSCI's fundamental concerns," he said, calling for credible free-float data, ownership disclosure and transparent engagement with international institutional investors.
"The biggest risk is not simply losing Emerging Market status, but letting doubts about market integrity become a lasting increase in Indonesia's cost of capital."

articles.title: 'Cannot play hide and seek': Minister's warning over haze sends Singapore agricultural stocks lower

paras.en: Shares of several Singapore-listed agricultural companies fell Tuesday after Senior Minister K Shanmugam warned they won't "escape responsibility" for their possible role in the haze blanketing the city-state.
"Companies cannot play hide and seek" with different corporate structures, hoping that will help them, Shanmugam said, revealing that seven companies had been questioned by the Singapore Exchange.
Bumitama Agri fell as much as 6.5%, while First Resources dropped to a low of 4.83%. Golden Agri Resources and Wilmar International slipped almost 2%.

Shanmugam, who is also home affairs minister for the city-state, said that some of the fires or smoke source points seem to be associated with First Resources, Bumitama Agri, as well as non-listed First Borneo Plantations.

"Take, for example, First Resources. It issued a detailed statement on its zero burning policy and firefighting efforts ... but statements, no matter how well drafted, are not good enough. Show us the evidence."
The other companies named by the minister were Golden Agri-Resources, Wilmar International, Kencana Agri, Indofood Agri and TSH Resources.
The haze has affected businesses and daily life in Singapore and Malaysia in the past few weeks, with the air quality in Singapore hitting levels not seen since 2015.
Schools in the state of Johor Bahru in Malaysia have also closed due to the air quality reaching unhealthy levels.

"They should not underestimate the Singapore government's determination to act," Shanmugam said, adding, "we will use every legal and regulatory lever at our disposal to exert pressure where it matters, including on their bottom lines, including on their access to financing, and including on their standing with investors."

He also revealed that Singapore could even amend laws or introduce new laws "on an urgent basis" to ensure cooperation, if needed. Companies potentially linked to the haze would also be examined if they still meet the standards for government grants or incentives.

When asked if Singapore's actions will affect bilateral relations between the city-state and Jakarta, Shanmugam dismissed the concern, saying, "Our people are suffering. What do these experts think we are supposed to do? Shiver in our shoes before we take any action to protect our own people? That's not the Singapore approach."

He was responding to a question about an article published by local media outlet CNA, which cited legal experts saying that actions taken by Singapore against haze-causing firms in Indonesia may carry diplomatic implications.

"If we think like that, there will be no Singapore, and we do not think there should be any bilateral issues. The Indonesian public is suffering as well, and it is in Indonesia's interests as much as ours to deal with the companies that are causing these problems."
He said that Singapore's actions against companies are aligned with the broad policies of Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto.
"In fact, we hope to get full cooperation from Indonesia in going after the companies," Shanmugam added

articles.title: Alarm grows over Russian satellite’s provocative approach to U.S.-owned satellite

paras.en: A Russian satellite came dangerously close to a Finnish-American satellite this weekend in a provocative maneuver that could foreshadow the new norm for space warfare.

According to public orbital tracking data, KOSMOS-2612, a Russian satellite launched in April with very few details disclosed, approached too close for comfort to ICEYE-X36, an imaging satellite from the Finnish company ICEYE that is owned by its U.S. subsidiary and has been used by the Ukrainian military. Nobody knows quite what KOSMOS-2612 did or what its intentions were, but the two satellites were, at most, a few hundred meters apart, with some estimates putting the distance at within 30 meters. Though the exact distance is unclear, the encounter still appears to be the closest known deliberate and uninvited interaction between two active spacecraft in low-Earth orbit.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: No explanatory or corroborating statements have emerged from Russian or U.S. defense officials or from ICEYE, leaving outside experts to speculate about the apparent orbital game of cat and mouse that unfolded overhead.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

Such a maneuver is not inherently aggressive or ill-intentioned, says Victoria Samson, head of space policy at the Secure World Foundation. But when taken in the context, the close approach is concerning.

“You’re looking at what Russia is doing here, not in terms, specifically, of what’s happening in space but as part of a larger examination of what’s happening on Earth,” Samson says. “Russia and Ukraine are literally at war with each other. And so it’s kind of tinting how you view Russia’s activities here.”

This maneuver is known as a rendezvous and proximity operation (RPO), and it’s not quite as straightforward as the simple formation flying that is routinely performed with airplanes. To get close to another object in orbit, a spacecraft needs to get itself into the same orbital plane and then change its velocity until it essentially matches the speed as its target so that the two don’t just zoom by each other.

Besides raising the odds of a catastrophic collision, such maneuvers usually require burning a lot of propellant, which is a nonrenewable resource. So satellite operators tend to only attempt them for very compelling reasons. In this case, the reason seems obvious: Russian officials have been unhappy about Ukraine’s purported use of ICEYE-X36’s synthetic aperture radar imaging, which can see through clouds and smoke to track and guide activity on the ground below. A Ukrainian official confirmed to Axios that the nation’s military works with the Finnish satellite company, and ICEYE announced earlier this year that it had signed a collaborative agreement with Ukraine’s defense ministry. ICEYE-X36 launched in 2024, two years after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: KOSMOS-2612’s stalking could be chiefly a warning meant to signal capability, or it could instead be intended for more direct and nefarious action: During an RPO, an aggressor satellite can do any number of things to its target, including taking pictures, jamming communications, blocking sensors or even physically disabling and pushing the other spacecraft out of orbit. Under pressure, the operators of ICEYE-X36 could well decide the spacecraft must burn precious propellant of its own to escape or elude KOSMOS-2612 or other threatening satellites, shortening the mission’s operational lifetime.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Russia’s maneuver has also come as Ukraine has faced broader interference with space-based support for its defense against Russia’s ongoing invasion: Ukrainian war fighters and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky have reported widespread throttling of SpaceX’s satellite-based Starlink and Starshield services on the battlefield.

The technology to accomplish RPOs is rapidly improving: China, the U.S., Russia and several private companies have all been independently testing their RPO capabilities for the past several years. Radar tracking data show that, since May, other KOSMOS satellites have been maneuvering around ICEYE-X36 in provocative maneuvers that have been explicitly called out by the U.S. Space Force.

There are few official international regulations related to these types of maneuvers, and conducting one nonconsensually breaks norms and crosses ill-defined lines for mutual safe operations on-orbit, Samson says. Unsolicited RPOs might be interpreted as aggressive—or even as an act of war. And already high tensions on the high frontier now seem set to soar: last month the U.S. Space Force announced that it had placed weapons in space. (The U.S. did not disclose many other details about the weapons, but some experts believe they’re communication jammers with RPO capabilities.)
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Although ground-based surveillance now allows close tracking of most satellites, without public statements from operators of secretive spacecraft, it’s harder to know what, exactly, they’re up to when conducting maneuvers such as this one. Samson says there’s little to do, for now, besides watching the mysterious drama play out overhead.
“We’re going to wait and see what happens,” she says. “This kind of thing can change quickly, but I would hold off hysterical speculation until we know more about it.”

articles.title: Japan launches a probe to collect rocks from Mars’s moon Phobos

paras.en: Japan’s mission to collect samples from a Martian moon is off to a good start.

Launched atop an H3 rocket from Tanegashima Space Center just after 3:40 P.M. EDT on Monday, the Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) mission is a collaboration between the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), NASA, the French space agency CNES and the European Space Agency (ESA).

If successful, MMX will be the first spacecraft to enter orbit around Phobos, one of Mars’s two moons. The goal is to learn more about how the mysterious, small moon first formed. One theory posits that Phobos and its companion, Deimos, are former asteroids that were captured by Mars’s gravity, while another is that they are composed of debris from an ancient, massive collision with the Red Planet.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The mission could also provide clues into how organic matter, or even life itself, forms on planets.

To figure this out, MMX will spend a year flying through space, and it is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in September 2027. Once there, it will observe the Martian moon from orbit to look for two suitable landing and sampling sites, one on each side of the natural satellite. Once those sites are found, the main spacecraft will release a rover, called Idefix, onto Phobos’s surface.

The rover will first sample material from Phobos’s subsurface in its onboard lab. Later the main spacecraft will land on Phobos sometime in 2030 and gather material in its return module. That module will lift off from Mars and come back to Earth with at least 10 grams of material sometime in 2031.

“Bringing samples to our most sophisticated labs here on Earth is a multiplier for discoveries, because our most precise instruments are too large, complex or sensitive to send to space,” said ESA’s MMX project scientist Elliot Sefton-Nash in a statement. “Even after the mission has been completed, future generations of scientists will study the Phobos samples with even more advanced instruments—samples brought to Earth are the gift that keeps on giving.”

articles.title: Can AI predict whether you’ll die from cancer from just an image of your face?

paras.en: A new artificial intelligence model can predict a cancer patient’s risk of dying from a single photograph of their face, according to new research. While not perfectly accurate, the model found that people with higher risk-of-death scores, in general, had a higher risk of dying.
The AI builds on how human doctors evaluate their patients’ health, says Ray Mak, a radiation oncologist at Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute, who conducted the research with his colleagues.

“We’re trained in medical school to walk into a room, look at the patient and make an assessment—an impression of how healthy, frail or sick they are,” Mak says. That decision can help determine what treatment a patient receives—surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, and more. The problem, Mak says, is “that’s really a subjective assessment.”

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The AI, Mak and his team hope, could help doctors and patients make more informed, objective decisions about cancer treatment and end-of-life care.

Mak and his colleagues trained an algorithm to analyze and “learn” 40 million images of faces without giving it a specific task. They then tweaked the model to analyze new photographs in two distinct ways: first, to estimate a person’s biological age and, second, to predict cancer patients’ odds of survival.

The outcome was surprisingly accurate. In a test group of 3,820 cancer patients, more than half of those with the highest risk score—64 out of 122—died within just 90 days of when their photograph was taken. In a separate test group that included more than 38,000 cancer patients, those that looked older than their chronological age also had a higher risk of dying.

“To our knowledge, this is the first report of an AI algorithm that can directly predict cancer patient survival from a simple face photograph,” the researchers write in the study, which was published on Monday in the journal Lancet Digital Health.

The question is: How does the AI do this? For both age and death risk predictions, Mak and his team tracked where the algorithm was “looking” in its analysis, a technique they call “attention mapping.” For age prediction, they found that the AI tended to base its predictions on facial areas such as the nasolabial folds—the crease between your nose and mouth—and parts of the forehead. For risk of death, the AI tended to focus on the bridge of the nose and areas below the eyes. It’s unclear why those areas specifically correlated with a person’s risk of death.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The two analyses work better together. “When we put both the face age and face survival scores into a clinical prognostic model, we do better at survival prediction than either one alone,” Mak says.

In some cases, the AI may have been picking up on known health risks, such as smoking and alcohol use. When it came to the age estimate, smokers, for instance, were more likely to look older than their age, Mak says. The same was true of heavy alcohol drinkers.

It also didn’t matter if a photograph showed a person frowning or smiling, with or without makeup or in various lighting. For age prediction, the AI was able to account for common forms of plastic surgery, Mak says. A major exception was rhinoplasty—the AI tended to rate people who’d had a nose job as slightly older in images taken after the surgery compared with images taken before it.

Mak’s hope is that, eventually, an AI model like this could be deployed in hospitals and serve as an extra data point in doctors’ decision-making. It could also help serve as an early-warning system of disease if a patient appears to be aging faster than expected. Mass General Brigham has a patent pending for face health algorithms.

Right now the AI is not ready for the clinic. For one, the cancer survival model was trained on a Boston-area cancer patient population that was majority white. Mak and his colleagues are working to expand their training sets to include a wider diversity of faces. (To that end, if you feel comfortable doing so, you can help train the algorithm and receive a “face age” estimate by sharing your own photographs here.)
But the possibility of AI having any role in determining a patient’s treatment plan raises clear ethical questions.

Matthew Liao, a professor and director of the Center for Bioethics at New York University, who was not involved in the new research, says that the paper was “interesting” and that this kind of tool could be useful for identifying people who might be sick and in need of extra care. But he notes it’s possible that an AI algorithm could slip up—and misidentify patients as being healthy or not. “If it gets it wrong, we might be sort of not providing care to someone who actually needs it,” he says.

Liao also raised the question of insurance companies turning to this sort of technology to grant or deny coverage or employers using it to hire a given job candidate deemed to be “healthier” than another. “We really need to think through the societal implications of this thing as we try as we develop it further,” he says.
Mak, for his part, is optimistic. “There’s still a lot of development ahead and clinical testing,” he says. “But we’re really excited that that we’re launching a completely new field in medicine.”

articles.title: To turn invisible, we need to tweak the path light travels
articles.author: Sofia Caetano Avritzer

paras.en: It’s pretty hard to fight an opponent you can’t see. That’s what makes Invisible Woman an invaluable member of the Fantastic Four. She can disappear in the blink of an eye and take out entire factions of enemies, all while her adversaries kick and punch empty air.

Characters with invisibility powers — Marvel Comics’ Invisible Woman (aka Sue Storm), H.G. Wells’ Invisible Man and The Incredibles’ Violet Parr — can do all sorts of cool things. Escape embarrassing situations. Snoop on other people. Go places where they’re not allowed.
Short of a theoretical invisibility cloak, that kind of lurking is impossible for us. But some animals can hide in plain sight by turning nearly transparent.

Invisibility is useful for animals that spend a lot of time in places with no good hiding spots, such as the air or open ocean, says Kate Feller, a visual ecologist at Union College in Schenectady, N.Y.

The secret to invisibility is all about light. “The way we see things is when light is reflected back off of an object onto our eyes,” Feller says. The more light that can pass through something undisturbed, the harder it is to see that thing.
Light can’t easily pass through most animals, but those with nearly invisible body parts have tricks to get around this hurdle.

Animals get their colors from pigments, compounds that appear as different colors depending on which wavelengths of light they absorb and which they reflect. Green pigments, for instance, reflect green light and absorb all other colors. Invisibility requires getting rid of these colorful compounds.

Most baby fish lack pigments at first, helping them hide from predators. Some species stay see-through their whole lives. One is the ghost catfish (Kryptopterus vitreolus). With a body that’s fully transparent from gills to tail, it looks like a floating head from afar.

It’s hard to hide every body part, though. Eyes need light-absorbing pigments to see. And even clear stomachs will show up if animals eat colorful food. A ghost catfish eats only small bits of food and its long, thin, tubelike stomach stretches out a meal, helping the organ stay hidden, says Qibin Zhao, a physicist and materials scientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University in China. Blood can’t be transparent either due to the iron-rich hemoglobin molecules that carry oxygen. So up close, the ghost catfish’s blood vessels are still visible.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But even pigment-free objects are not entirely invisible. Light travels at different speeds through different materials so will bend or bounce when it goes from one material to another. That can create a shine, like sun reflecting off a puddle.

That’s not a big problem for a glasswing butterfly (Greta oto): Its wings have fewer reflective scales than other butterflies’ wings. The wings are also covered in tiny wax bumps that make light’s transition from air to tissue more gradual, so light passes through the wings mostly undisturbed.

Invisible Woman uses a completely different vanishing trick than real-life transparent animals. Instead of letting light pass through her, she bends lights rays to completely avoid her body. The rays never even touch her, so they are not reflected or absorbed, making her invisible to any onlookers.

In 2006, scientists proposed that this same logic could be used to create an invisibility cloak. But in practice, a material that perfectly bends light rays is expensive, hard to make and can divert only a narrow band of light at a time. That’s just enough to make a single-colored object disappear but not an entire human.

And there’s another problem: With no light getting into the cloak, a person inside can’t see out. Luckily, Sue Storm has the ability to use cosmic rays to see while she’s invisible, allowing her to protect the world from supervillains like Doctor Doom.

articles.title: Brain implants are helping people who’ve lost their voice
articles.author: Laura Sanders

paras.en: On paper, my interview with Casey Harrell looks like any other.

I ask the questions, he answers them. He tells me about his background as a climate activist, his Southern roots and his daughter, who as a preschooler loved to dress up like a cheetah and roar around the house. “My daughter was incredibly cute in her cheetah outfit,” Harrell says.
The transcript tells the story of our conversation. But between the lines is an entirely different story — the story of where Harrell’s words come from.

Harrell started losing his ability to speak in his early 40s, nearly six years ago. He talked to me using a brain implant that can decode his words directly from his thoughts. The device, called a brain-computer interface, is experimental. But it has transformed Harrell’s life. And it could soon transform others. Advances in computing power and AI, lessons gleaned from patient experience and investments from neurotechnology companies are starting to yield real progress on brain-computer interfaces for people who can no longer talk. In other words, Harrell’s new voice might not be so singular in the future.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “There’s a lot of excitement and hope in the field right now,” says Matthew Willsey, a neurosurgeon and biomedical engineer at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, who recently implanted a new type of speech interface in a woman’s brain. For years, Willsey says, scientists didn’t know whether attempts to decode speech would be successful; now, a body of research results points clearly to yes. “They’re thinking, ‘Wow, this is actually a usable technology that addresses a real problem that people suffer from.’”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Harrell has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS. The progressive neurodegenerative disease, which affects an estimated 35,000 people in the United States, kills nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord that control muscles. As the neural connections between Harrell’s brain and body began to falter, he gradually lost his ability to move his muscles, leaving him confined to his bed or a wheelchair. Some of those dropped signals directed the muscles in his throat and mouth, the ones that allow him to speak.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “I began to lose my ability to talk shortly after my diagnosis in 2020,” Harrell says. After that, it was “a slow-motion car crash” as fewer and fewer people could understand him. “[My voice] is the most important thing I have lost in this whole disease,” he says.

In a stroke of luck, Harrell learned through a family member about a clinical trial happening at the University of California, Davis — one that attempted to restore speech with a brain-computer interface. In 2023, Harrell had four small devices implanted on the left side of his brain. These grids of electrodes reside on Harrell’s speech motor cortex, a stretch of brain along the precentral gyrus that controls the movements required for speech.

Today, Harrell uses his system for about 10 to 14 hours daily, making him, as he puts it, “the world’s biggest power user of the brain-to-computer interface known to man.” Hard data suggest he’s right. A recent count shows that Harrell has used his system to communicate nearly 2 million words, the scientists working with him reported in June in Nature Medicine.

The very existence of Harrell’s words shows it may be possible to restore speech for people with ALS, as well as for those whose speech is impaired by stroke, paralysis, cerebral palsy and Parkinson’s disease. “This kind of technology has the potential to dramatically change the conversation,” says David Brandman, a UC Davis neurosurgeon and neuroscientist who works with Harrell.
Harrell’s interface still has room for improvement. It’s bulky, relatively slow and limited in what sorts of nonword sounds it can decode.

But it is a “beginning,” says Leigh Hochberg, a neuroscientist at Brown University who works with Harrell. “It’s still early days. There’s a lot of research to happen, and it’s going to be very exciting.” The end game, Hochberg says, is a world in which people could use a device to communicate seamlessly, quickly, clearly — and in their former voices.

Success would mean restoring more than just people’s words, Brandman says. It would mean restoring their ability to connect in all the ineffable ways that make us human. “Speech is so fundamental to who we are,” he says. “Imagine living in a world where you couldn’t tell someone you’re in pain, or you couldn’t say that you love them … It’s not hard to imagine how devastating that would be for your quality of life.”

On the path to a technology that enables fast, natural speech, scientists first had to answer a more basic question: Could the brain’s electrical chatter be decoded and translated into action outside of the head?

Nerve cells speak to each other with tiny pulses of electricity, signals that can be picked up with electrodes. The existence of this electrical language raised the tantalizing idea that electrical messages could be decoded straight from where they originate in the brain, bypassing damaged links to the rest of the body.

“This has really started as early as the 1950s, the first time scientists put electrodes into brains to record neural activity,” says Sergey Stavisky, a neuroscientist and neural engineer at UC Davis. “You can record the electrical activity of brain cells or parts of the brain. And that’s really when modern neuroscience started trying to study, how does the brain compute? How does it allow us to move our muscles?”

Figuring out how to decode simple neural commands was the first step. Animal studies paved the way, including experiments in which rhesus monkeys consciously controlled the movements of a robotic arm using only brain signals detected by implanted electrodes.
The Deep End podcast explores what makes your voice yours

What if you lost your voice? Today, AI can re-create it, and brain implants can turn thoughts into speech. This season of The Deep End follows people living through these vocal transformations — and asks what these remarkable technologies can teach us about why our voices matter in the first place.

By 2004, scientists had enough confidence in the approach to launch a clinical trial in humans called BrainGate. Researchers implanted a grid of electrodes in the brain of a paralyzed man named Matthew Nagle. A former star athlete, Nagle was able to control a computer cursor with his thoughts alone. “That was really the starting gun of the modern version of the brain-computer interface field,” Stavisky says.

From there, attempts to link brain activity with some physical outcome — such as moving a computer mouse, a wheelchair or a robotic arm — blossomed. Some of these efforts focused on the brain signals and regions that controlled movements of the hands and arms. Others focused on a very tricky version of the same basic problem: talking.

A brain-computer interface that could detect the intention to say a word and bypass the muscles needed to say it would be a powerful workaround for people with diseases like ALS or brain injuries. And it is no small thing to people who can no longer talk. “Losing their speech is way more devastating than losing their mobility,” says Jessica Pietrowski, a speech and language pathologist at UC Davis who has worked with many such patients. “Speech is how they maintain their identity in their relationships.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Harrell emphasizes this point. “What does my voice mean to me? It means so much,” he says. “It is the ability to parent my daughter. It is the ability to connect with my wife. It is the ability to make a wry joke with my friends.”

Talking feels effortless to most of us, but just saying hello involves a sweeping array of actions — and upwards of 100 muscles. “It’s incredibly complex and intricate, and really, an incredible human feat,” Pietrowski says.

Consider the “h” sound in “hello.” Known as a glottal fricative, it involves an orchestra of tiny movements. First, the diaphragm contracts to fill the lungs with air. Chest and abdominal muscles push air up through relaxed vocal cords and surrounding tissues. This puff of air then travels to the mouth, where lips, jaw and tongue execute complex sequences of movements that create the rest of the sound. Finally, air waves, perfectly shaped, ripple from the mouth. Then, and only then, “you have speech,” Pietrowski says.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But the beginnings of this nearly miraculous transformation start in the brain, where tiny electrical nerve pulses command the body to speak. In Harrell’s trial, he would attempt to speak words, prompting his motor cortex to send signals to his body. The implanted electrodes would detect the patterns and send them to a computer to interpret. With this work-around, it didn’t matter that Harrell’s muscles didn’t get the message; the computer would.

After Harrell recovered from surgery, researchers began testing the system in his home. They collected his neural data and streamed it to computers on a nearby cart, where machine learning algorithms attempted to match Harrell’s brain activity patterns to those that predictably occur with certain sounds. Called phonemes, these sound units are the building blocks of words. The algorithm assembled the phonemes into words, as it made its best guess about what Harrell was trying to say. To limit the computational power required, the algorithm used a vocabulary of just 50 words.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: When the system was plugged in and ready to go, scientists asked Harrell to try and say a specific, random sentence built from that library: “What good is that?”
Harrell got to work. His eyebrows shot up as he saw the words appear on a screen in front of him in response to his thoughts. The decoder worked.

Everyone paused. Some of the researchers started to cry. Harrell and his family became emotional. Being in the room when the switch was flipped on was “incredible,” Brandman says. “The majority of my adult life was working up to that moment, and to see it come to fruition was an incredible experience. But more than that was seeing what impact it immediately had for Casey and his family.”

Harrell remembers his feelings that day, too: “Pure joy.” Even though he wasn’t choosing his words for that first test, “it was a profound moment,” he says. “The possibilities for the near future for me and the rest of humanity were overwhelming to realize.”

The second day of testing was even more profound, but in a personal way. This time, the system’s algorithm was using a vocabulary of over 125,000 words. This would be more challenging for the decoder, but it would give Harrell more autonomy to say what he wanted.
Harrell started the session with a joke, Hochberg recalls, along the lines of, “Is this thing on?” But his next line was a real puzzler: “I’m looking for a cheetah.”

Hochberg, who had joined remotely on a video call, was sure it was a mistake. “There’s no way that the second sentence on the second day of using a brain-to-computer interface is going to say anything about a cheetah,” Hochberg says. “That’s obviously a decoding error.”
But there was something the scientist couldn’t see. Harrell’s 4-year-old daughter had bounded into the room, dressed as a cheetah.

The discovery was big scientifically, but it was bigger for what it represented to Harrell. Brain technology could restore not just his words, but also the spontaneous exchanges that had once made up his everyday life.
“It was so amazing to be able to be understood right from the get-go and to be able to talk and respond to my daughter,” Harrell says, “especially because that was lacking completely from my life.”

Hochberg says moments like that represent the promise that brain-computer interfaces hold. “To me, seeing it work that quickly and that powerfully really, really emphasized that these are technologies that are going to be able to restore not only activities of daily living,” he says, “but they’re going to restore communication between parent and child.”
Casey Harrell’s brain-computer interface extracts neural signals from his brain and, through a few key steps, transforms them into

words. Electrodes implanted in Harrell’s speech motor cortex detect neurons’ electrical signals (1), generating raw neural data (2). Advanced machine learning efforts (3) map chunks of the data to phonemes, the building blocks of words (4). Those phonemes are then assembled into sentences by a predictive language model, or LM (5), and put on a screen where they can be read or spoken.

Harrell uses his interface to send email and Slack messages and play Wordle with his wife and child. He uses it to work; in fact, he’s just getting started on a new climate consultancy project. Harrell’s interface has connected him to the world in a way that would have been impossible even a few years ago.

But the system is still a research device. And like any early design, it comes with limitations. First, it isn’t portable; Harrell has wires coming from a port that sits on the top of his head, and he can use it only at home. And it is slow by the standards of typical conversation. You can’t tell from the written transcript of our interview, but our conversations always came with built-in delays.
For example, as we chatted, we discovered that we had both worked in the same part of Washington, D.C. I asked him if he remembered his old address. The answer came some two minutes later.

“I make a very simple analogy where I talk about having the brain-to-computer interface being akin to trying to catch a train, running to get the last car before it leaves the station,” Harrell says. With the current interface, “if people are patient and wait for my sentence correction, I can [catch the train and] be a part of the conversation.”

Harrell’s system translates his neural activity into words on a screen. If he chooses to do so, he can then use a computerized voice to say the words out loud. “It is brain-to-text, and then it gets translated to the voice,” Harrell says. A brain-to-voice system, in which a person’s thoughts are translated directly into spoken words, he adds, “is the holy grail of what this will become.”

Harrell and the scientists working with him are getting closer to this very type of real-time communication. Last year in Nature, they debuted a new algorithm that attempted to turn Harrell’s brain signals straight into sounds. The results: He could speak his mind with a delay of just 10 milliseconds. That’s very close to a real-time conversation. But the sounds Harrell made were hard to understand, with just over half of them being intelligible to listeners.

The next generation of devices aims to do better. Willsey, the University of Michigan neurosurgeon, is working on one such device, a fully implantable array. In June, he implanted what’s called the “cortical module,” about the size of a dime, in the brain of a 68-year-old woman. Like Harrell, the woman could no longer talk in a way that most people could understand.

Unlike the BrainGate system, this new device — made by Austin, Texas–based neurotechnology company Paradromics — is portable. Surgeons implanted it in a stretch of brain tissue that made up the woman’s speech motor cortex, along the precentral gyrus. The cortical module collects neural data and sends it to another device implanted in the chest called a transceiver. From there, signals shoot to a receiver on her chest, where the data gets transformed into sounds — spoken words that play out of speakers on a nearby computer.
